opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the representational properties of circuits themselves. A deep network is essentially a very large circuit, and circuits are a fairly weak representational language. They don't have the expressive power of, say, first-order logic or a general programming language. So if you want to represent something like the rules of Go, which you can write down in a page of a programming language with quantifiers like "for every square on the board" or "for every adjacent stone," a circuit has to unroll all of that. It has to represent the same piece of knowledge over and over again at every location, every time step, every instance. That means the circuit can be enormously larger than the underlying concept, and, crucially, you need an enormous amount of data to learn all those copies, because each one has to be learned somewhat independently.

That shows up empirically. These systems are remarkably data-hungry. A human child learns language from a tiny fraction of the text a large language model sees, and people learn a game like Go from a handful of examples and an explanation of the rules. That gap in sample efficiency isn't just a matter of engineering; I think it reflects the fact that the system isn't learning the compact, general representation.

And there's evidence that what they learn is brittle. A few years ago, some researchers found that superhuman Go programs could be beaten by fairly amateur players using a particular strategy, building a large group and encircling it. The programs had never correctly learned the concept of a group of stones being alive or dead in general. They'd learned a huge patchwork of approximations that worked in the positions they'd seen. If a system with millions of games of self-play can't reliably learn a concept that basic, you have to ask what's happening with much more complicated concepts in the real world.

So my view is that scaling up gives you better and better approximations, and they can be extremely useful, but you get diminishing returns. You run out of high-quality data, the compute costs grow, and you still have these strange failures off the training distribution. To get past that, I think we'll need systems that combine learning with more expressive representations, things like probabilistic programming, where you can express general knowledge compactly, reason with it, and learn from far less data. That's not to say deep learning goes away; it'll likely be an important component. But I don't think simply making the circuits bigger gets us to general-purpose intelligence.

r001.rationale: It says circuits must unroll a general rule and represent the same knowledge repeatedly across locations, time steps, and instances.

r002.rationale: It links the repeated copies to needing enormous amounts of data because each copy must be learned somewhat independently.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss evolutionary search over programs or whether that approach is practically plausible.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start by saying that I don't think it's going to stop working. Deep learning will keep producing impressive results, and the systems we have now are genuinely useful. The question is whether this particular approach, where you take a fixed circuit, a network of simple units with weighted connections, and you tune those weights with enormous amounts of data, is a path all the way to general-purpose intelligence. And I think the answer is no, for reasons that have to do with what a circuit fundamentally is.

A circuit is a very poor representation for a lot of the knowledge that intelligent behavior requires. Take something as simple as the rules of Go. You can write them down in a few lines of first-order logic. A circuit has no way to express "for all positions on the board" or "for all stones in a group." It has to effectively unroll that generalization into a separate chunk of network for every location. So you end up with systems that have played millions of games, far more than any human, and yet, as we've seen with some of the adversarial work on AlphaZero-style programs, they still fail to grasp concepts that a human beginner picks up in an afternoon, like what a group of stones is and whether it's alive or dead. They've learned something that approximates the right function over the data they've seen, but they haven't learned the concept.

That's the crux of it. Circuits are good at what I'd call pattern completion. They are not good at representing composable, reusable, general knowledge, and they're not good at the kind of reasoning that operates on that knowledge, where you chain together many steps and each step depends on the result of the last. Humans, and for that matter the earlier tradition in AI, use expressive representations, things like logic and probabilistic programs, precisely because a few general facts can do the work of an astronomically large number of specific cases. The circuit approach gives that up, and the price is that you need data and compute that scale exponentially with the complexity of the task.

So people say, well, we'll just make the networks bigger. And that's been the story of the last several years. But I'd point out that the amount of text we're training on is already most of what humanity has ever written, and the energy budgets are approaching the output of small countries. If the gains were coming from a better understanding of intelligence, you'd expect the curve to look different. Instead it looks like what you'd expect from a representation that doesn't generalize efficiently, where you compensate by brute force. Brute force has a limit, and I think we're closer to it than the enthusiasm suggests.

There's also a deeper point, which is that we don't actually know what these systems are doing internally, and that matters both for capability and for safety. If you can't inspect the knowledge, you can't correct it, you can't verify it, and you can't be sure the objective the system is pursuing is the one you intended. So I'd expect the next real advances to come from combining learning with explicit representations, systems that can learn structured models of the world and reason with them, rather than from stacking more layers onto a circuit and hoping intelligence falls out.

r001.rationale: It says circuits cannot express rules such as “for all positions” and must unroll them into separate network chunks for each location.

r002.rationale: It links that need to represent cases separately to requiring enormous data and compute, which scale exponentially with task complexity.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss evolutionary search over programs or distinguish its theoretical possibility from practical plausibility.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental limitation is that a circuit carries out a fixed amount of computation. You put the inputs in, they propagate through the layers, and an answer comes out. Making the circuit bigger gives you more computation, but it doesn’t give you the ability to decide, for a particular problem, how much computation is needed.

Suppose I ask you a mathematical question. You might answer it immediately, or you might need a piece of paper and several hours, or you might work on it for years. That flexibility—the ability to construct and execute a process of reasoning—is a very important part of intelligence.

Now, you can put a neural network inside a system that runs it repeatedly, maintains memory, and searches over possible solutions. So this isn’t an argument that neural networks are useless. It’s an argument that learning an enormous input-output mapping is not, by itself, a sufficient account of intelligence. We need systems that can compose what they know and carry out computations whose structure and length depend on the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says a circuit performs a fixed amount of computation, but does not say circuit-based representations cannot state one shared rule for all applicable instances.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute large training-data requirements to learning cases separately instead of generalizing a rule.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss evolutionary search over programs or distinguish theoretical possibility from practical plausibility.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the basic issue is that a fixed circuit is a rather limited form of computation. A neural network takes an input and passes it through some number of layers to produce an output. But many of the things we want intelligence to do require a variable amount of computation. If I give you a mathematical problem, you might need ten steps of reasoning, or a million. You don’t know in advance.

Now, you can make the circuit bigger, and you can train it on more examples. That can take you a surprisingly long way. But it doesn’t by itself give you a general mechanism for carrying out an arbitrarily long computation, maintaining the intermediate results, and deciding what to do next.

So I would distinguish between neural networks as useful components of an intelligent system and the claim that scaling up a fixed circuit is sufficient for intelligence. The former seems very plausible. The latter seems to me to leave out a great deal of what we mean by reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says fixed circuits are limited in variable-length computation, but does not say they cannot express a shared rule applying across instances.

r002.rationale: It mentions training on more examples, but does not attribute data requirements to learning cases separately instead of applying a generalized rule.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss evolutionary search over programs or whether that approach is practically plausible.
